What the provided material does establish: Lightning Bolt’s oracle text is “Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target,” so Lightning Bolt can target a player or a planeswalker ([115.4]; Lightning Bolt). Vivien Reid is a planeswalker card (Vivien Reid). The rules also describe redirection effects (they are replacement effects that can replace damage dealt to one object with damage dealt to another) and note that the old automatic player→planeswalker redirection rule was removed ([614.9]; [306.7]). Some rules explain how effects that let a player change targets operate (they exist and follow specific processes) ([115.7b]; [115.7f]). Replacement effects and prevention effects watch for events and replace or prevent them as they happen ([801.13a]; [614.1]; [615.1]).

What’s missing and why I can’t conclude: the specific rules that define when targets are chosen and become fixed (the targeting rules that say whether targets are chosen when the spell is cast and whether the caster may choose a different valid target at resolution), and the rules that say what happens if a spell’s target is or becomes illegal at resolution. If you can provide the rules that define when targets are chosen/locked in and how spells behave if targets change or are illegal at resolution, I can apply them to this exact situation and give a definitive answer.

Definitions

- Redirection effect: a replacement effect that causes damage that would be dealt to one creature, planeswalker, or player to be dealt instead to another creature, planeswalker, or player ([614.9]).
entries.answer_gold: No. Lightning Bolt deals damage to its target, Nola. There is no rule that allows damage dealt to a player to be redirected to a planeswalker.

A player may turn a manifested permanent they control face up as a special action any time they have priority and, if it’s a creature card, they do so by paying that card’s mana cost [701.40b] and [Soul Summons].
- Mutate / merging: When a mutating creature spell resolves targeting a legal creature, it merges with that target and the objects become one merged (mutated) permanent; the mutating spell’s object merges with the targeted permanent as it resolves [608.3d] and [702.140c]. Declare blockers is a single turn‑based action that doesn’t use the stack, so you can’t interleave casting Displace between declaring some blockers and declaring others [509.1]. If you tried to partially declare blockers, cast Displace, then finish declaring blockers, that would be an illegal action and would be reversed [733.1].

Even if Displace resolves after Ogre Resister is declared as a blocker for Frenzied Raptor, Exile and return from Displace removes Ogre Resister from combat (objects that leave the battlefield are removed from combat), so Ogre Resister would stop being a blocking creature when exiled and would return to the battlefield not as a blocking creature unless an effect specifically put it onto the battlefield blocking [506.4; Displace]. Because Displace’s returned creatures aren’t put onto the battlefield “blocking” (Displace simply returns them to the battlefield), the returned Ogre Resister won’t be a blocking creature on return [509.4a]. And once the declare‑blockers action is finished you can’t declare additional blockers for that combat step [509.1; 509.1g/h].

Definitions used:
- “Removed from combat”: a permanent is removed from combat if it leaves the battlefield, its controller changes, it phases out, an effect specifically removes it from combat, an attacking or blocking creature regenerates, stops being a creature, or becomes a battle; a creature removed from combat stops being an attacking, blocking, blocked, and/or unblocked creature [506.4].
- “Put onto the battlefield blocking”: a creature put onto the battlefield blocking by an effect is put onto the battlefield already blocking a chosen attacking creature (its controller chooses which), and such a creature is “blocking” though for trigger purposes it’s never considered to have “blocked” in the normal declare‑blockers action [509.4a].

Note about timing: if Natalie casts Displace before the declare‑blockers action (so Ogre Resister returns to the battlefield before blockers are declared), then during the subsequent single declare‑blockers action she could choose to declare Ogre Resister as the blocker for whichever attacking creature she chooses (for example, Knight Errant). The prohibition above only prevents interrupting the declare‑blockers action itself [509.1; 733.1].

By the time Natalie could cast Displace, the opportunity to declare blockers has already passed, so Ogre Resister wouldn't be able to block an additional creature.

Why: Legion Warboss’s ability instructs Amirah to “create a 1/1 red Goblin creature token” and further says “That token gains haste until end of turn and attacks this combat if able” (Legion Warboss). Creating a token is putting a token onto the battlefield (rule 701.7a). Divine Visitation replaces the creation of creature tokens under Amirah’s control with the creation of 4/4 white Angel creature tokens with flying and vigilance (Divine Visitation; [Divine Visitation ruling #2]). As the ruling explains, the created token’s characteristics are entirely replaced by a 4/4 white Angel with flying and vigilance and it doesn’t have the Goblin/1/1 characteristics, but “anything else specified in the effect creating the token (such as … ‘That token gains haste,’ or ‘attacking’) still applies” ([Divine Visitation ruling #2]). 

Because the creating effect still specifies that the token “gains haste until end of turn” and “attacks this combat if able,” the 4/4 white Angel token will get haste until end of turn and will be put onto the battlefield attacking this combat unless it is unable to attack. A creature put onto the battlefield attacking is considered to be attacking as it enters (rule 508.4c). Legion Warboss’s ruling confirms that if the token can’t attack for some reason (for example, it’s unable to attack or a cost to attack isn’t paid), then it doesn’t attack ([Legion Warboss ruling #2]).

Assumption about timing: I’m assuming the usual timing that Legion Warboss’s triggered ability resolved and then the token was created. If some other simultaneous replacement or control-changing effect applied, the order of those replacement effects could affect what’s created (see rules about replacement effects), but the provided card ruling for Divine Visitation already governs how Divine Visitation replaces the created token ([Divine Visitation ruling #2]).

Divine Visitation creates a replacement effect that replaces Legion Warboss's token with a different token. After it's created as a 4/4 Angel, it gains haste and an effect is created that requires it to attack.

Yes — Chalice of the Void will trigger. Shivan Fire has a mana value of 1, and Chalice of the Void has one charge counter, so the condition “a spell with mana value equal to the number of charge counters” is met. Paying the additional {1} imposed by Thorn of Amethyst doesn’t change Shivan Fire’s mana value; additional costs are paid in addition to a spell’s mana cost and aren’t part of its mana cost (they contribute to the spell’s total cost, not its mana value). Chalice of the Void looks at the spell’s mana value as the spell is cast and triggers if that value equals its charge counters, and Chalice of the Void must be on the battlefield at the end of casting for the ability to trigger — which is satisfied here.

Short reasoning and relevant points: 
- Shivan Fire’s printed mana value is 1, and Chalice of the Void has one charge counter, so the trigger condition is met. 
- Thorn of Amethyst’s “noncreature spells cost {1} more to cast” is an additional/cost-increasing effect that changes the spell’s total cost but does not change the spell’s mana cost or mana value. 
- The game determines total cost (mana cost plus additional costs) separately from the spell’s mana cost/mana value; Chalice of the Void’s trigger cares about mana value. 
- Chalice of the Void must be on the battlefield at the end of casting for its ability to trigger; if it were sacrificed as part of casting the spell, it couldn’t trigger.

entries.answer:
No. Dread’s “When Dread is put into a graveyard from anywhere, shuffle it into its owner’s library.” ability will not trigger in this situation because Yixlid Jailer causes cards in graveyards to lose all abilities and this kind of “from anywhere” zone-change trigger would trigger from the graveyard.

Explanation and definitions
- A “zone-change trigger” is a triggered ability that triggers when an object changes zones (for example, an ability that triggers when an object is put into a graveyard). The game determines where such an ability triggers from according to the specific wording of the ability [603.6].
- Dread’s ability triggers “when [it is] put into a graveyard from anywhere,” so that triggered ability would trigger from the graveyard when Dread is moved there [Dread ruling #2].
- Yixlid Jailer makes “cards in graveyards lose all abilities.” For abilities that trigger when the object is put into a graveyard from anywhere, Yixlid Jailer stops those abilities from triggering at all (they would be ones that would otherwise trigger from the graveyard) [Yixlid Jailer ruling #4].

Because Niko’s Ruin Processor ability put Dread from exile into Avianna’s graveyard, that is exactly the “from anywhere” event Dread’s ability cares about, but Yixlid Jailer prevents such a graveyard-triggering ability from triggering, so no trigger is created.

Assumption: I’m assuming the described sequence is that Ruin Processor’s ability moves Dread from exile to Avianna’s graveyard; the answer would be the same for any timing of that move (the key point is the move into the graveyard and Yixlid Jailer’s effect).
entries.answer_gold: No. Triggered abilities are checked to see if they trigger immediately after the event occurs. Dread does not have any abilities at that time.
